newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, U.S. jointly appeal for Zaire ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: France, U.S. jointly appeal for Zaire ceasefire.

text.p: France and the United States, at loggerheads for months over central Africa, appealed jointly on Tuesday for a ceasefire in Zaire as Tutsi rebels continued to sweep across the east of the country.

"We agreed on the need to act to resolve this crisis by applying the Security Council resolution and the first objective is a ceasefire on the ground, and the opening of negotiations involving all the parties," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said after talks with U.S. Assistant Secretary of State George Moose.

The top U.S. Africa expert said: "We share the same concern ...the need to act quickly, to support the action of (U.N. mediator Mohammed) Sahnoun, to achieve a cessation of hostilites and encourage all parties to get round a table soon and start serious negotiations."

Moose has been supporting diplomatic efforts by South Africa to arrange peace talks on Zaire, where rebels led by Laurent Kabila have captured more than a fifth of the country including the third-largest city, Kisangani.

France has long backed ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, 66, who is in hospital in Monaco for cancer treatment, despite opposition charges of rampant corruption under his three decades in power. It has urged sending international troops to help refugees, a plan opposed by Washington.
Both men said the best way to aid the hundreds of thousands of refugees, mainly Rwandan Hutus, trapped in eastern Zaire was to get a ceasefire and negotiations started.

French officials say that while the Kinshasa government has accepted the U.N. peace plan, which also provides for elections and an international conference on the Great Lakes region, Kabila has repeatedly refused to accept a ceasefire.
Moose also met officials in President Jacques Chirac's office.
Kabila, with little interest in a general ceasefire while his troops seem to be gaining the upper hand, vowed on Tuesday that his forces would take over Africa's third largest country.

He promised a temporary ceasefire for 20 km (13 miles) around the newly captured city of Kisangani to allow in humanitarian aid and let people who fled return, but said advances on all other fronts would continue.

Asked why Kabila should stop fighting when his forces were advancing with little resistance, Moose said: "It's hard to put oneself in Mr Kabila's place. The international community has an interest in stopping this violence and everyone wants a political solution. That's what Mr Kabila says, too."
In a marked change of tone, the United States voiced concern on Monday that the rebels were getting help and weapons from the governments of neighbouring Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda and Angola.

Mobutu, who has spent most of his time on the French Riviera since surgery for prostate cancer last year, was readmitted to hospital in Monaco at the weekend. His son and spokesman said he still planned to return home and quell the rebellion.
